title: AI and work: the evidence, in five mornings
subtitle: One payroll dataset, two field experiments, two classroom trials and the inside of Anthropic, so you can stop quoting LinkedIn in the team meeting

source.name: five public sources, linked in each lesson

made_with: Drafted by an AI from the sources themselves, then edited; every number and quote was checked against the original paper or page, with the link in the lesson.
audience: anyone who gets asked "so is AI going to take the jobs?" at dinner

days.title: The canaries: who is not being hired
days.hook: The most quoted labour paper of the AI era was revised in August 2026 with a year more of payroll data. Here is what it actually says.
days.lesson:
Canaries in the Coal Mine? by Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab uses administrative payroll data from ADP covering millions of US workers, now through June 2026. Six facts carry the paper. There is no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement. Employment of 22 to 25 year olds in the occupations most exposed to AI stands 19 percent below where it would be had it kept pace with their less-exposed peers, and experienced workers show no comparable gap. That divergence has widened steadily since the authors first documented it in August 2025. It works through reduced hiring of young people, not through layoffs. It is concentrated where AI is used to substitute for human tasks; where AI complements workers, employment is flat or rising, especially for experienced staff. And the adjustment happens through jobs, not through base pay.

You have probably seen 13 percent quoted. The two numbers are not the same measure: 13 was a regression estimate on July 2025 data; the revision reports a plain kept-pace gap, which was 15 percent at that vintage and 19 percent by June 2026. If you cite the paper, cite the measure.

The authors are careful about what this is: early, descriptive indicators, not a verdict. The patterns weaken when you control for education, some trends predate generative AI, and the ADP sample shows them more sharply than national surveys do. That honesty is the part worth copying.

For our clients the lesson is about where to look. Headcount in a ministry will not move first. The next cohort of hires, and the tasks they are no longer asked to do, will.

quote.text: employment of young workers in AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with that of their less-exposed peers, with no comparable gap for experienced workers
quote.where: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?, August 2026 version, introduction (fact 2 of six)

question.q: Through which channel does the paper say the gap for young workers mostly operates?
question.explain: Fact 4 in the paper: the divergence operates primarily through reduced hiring rather than increased separations, and fact 6 adds that adjustment happens through employment, not base compensation. Layoffs make the news; the empty desk that was never filled does not.

days.do: Think of the last three junior hires in your unit, or the ones that did not happen. Write one line on which of their tasks an AI now does. That is your own canary.

figure.caption: Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed jobs, relative to where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers. The gap widened in a year.
figure.where: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen, Canaries in the Coal Mine?, August 2026 version, introduction (PDF page 3)
figure.note: Experienced workers show no comparable gap.

days.title: The jagged frontier: 758 consultants
days.hook: A randomized experiment at BCG explains most of what you have felt using these tools: brilliant on one task, fluently wrong on the next.
days.lesson:
In 2023, Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Ethan Mollick, Karim Lakhani and colleagues ran a preregistered experiment with 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group (Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013). After a baseline, people were randomly assigned to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 plus a short prompting overview, and then given realistic consulting tasks.

On 18 tasks inside what the AI could do well, from creative to analytical, consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2 percent more tasks, finished them 25.1 percent faster and produced work of significantly higher quality. On one complex managerial task chosen to sit outside that boundary, the AI users were 19 percent less likely to produce the correct answer than the people without it. The authors called the boundary the jagged frontier: AI is excellent and poor at tasks that look equally hard to a human, and the line does not run where you would guess.

Two details matter for an office like ours. The gains were largest for the consultants who had scored lowest at baseline, so the tool compressed the gap between the best and the rest. And the prompting overview helped little; what helped was knowing which side of the line a task was on, which you only learn by checking the AI's work on tasks where you already know the answer.

The practical rule is unglamorous. Inside the frontier, delegate and verify lightly. Outside it, the same tool makes a fluent, well-formatted mistake, and fluency is exactly what you are not checking for.

quote.text: for a complex managerial task selected to be outside the frontier, subjects using AI were 19% less likely to produce correct solutions compared with those without AI
quote.where: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper 24-013 (2023), abstract

question.q: In the BCG experiment, what happened on the task chosen to sit outside the AI's frontier?
options: AI users were 19 percent less likely to be right
AI users were 12.2 percent faster but no more accurate
AI users and non-users did equally well
AI users produced higher quality but took longer
question.explain: The abstract reports that on the task outside the frontier, subjects using AI were 19 percent less likely to produce correct solutions. The 12.2 percent (more tasks) and 25.1 percent (faster) figures are the gains on the 18 tasks inside the frontier. Same tool, same people, opposite result: that is the jagged line.

days.do: Pick two tasks on your list today: one you are sure AI does well (a summary, a first draft) and one you are not sure about (a judgment call on a counterpart). Hand only the first to AI. Check the second against your own answer before you believe it.

figure.caption: Consultants with GPT-4 against consultants without it: better and faster on 18 tasks inside the frontier, less often right on the one task outside it.
figure.where: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, HBS Working Paper 24-013 (2023), abstract
figure.unit: Difference from the no-AI group, percent

cover.alt: First page of Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Organization Science

days.title: The cybernetic teammate: 776 at P&G
days.hook: The same team went to Procter and Gamble in 2025 and asked a different question: can one person with AI do the work of a pair?
days.lesson:
In The Cybernetic Teammate (NBER Working Paper 33641, 2025), Dell'Acqua, Mollick, Lakhani and colleagues ran a preregistered field experiment with 776 professionals at Procter and Gamble. People worked on real product innovation challenges, randomly assigned to work alone or in pairs, with or without AI. The pairs mixed the two tribes every company has: R&D and Commercial.

The headline: individuals with AI matched the performance of two-person teams without it. Teams with AI did better still. AI also dissolved the silos. Without it, R&D people proposed technical solutions and commercial people proposed commercial ones; with it, both produced balanced proposals regardless of their background. And people working with AI reported more positive emotions, which the authors read as the tool taking on part of the social and motivational role a teammate usually plays. Anyone who has written an aide-memoire alone at 11 pm will recognize the finding.

Put Morning 2 and Morning 3 together. Inside the frontier, one person with AI is a pair, and the pair with AI is a better pair. Outside it, the same person is fluent and wrong. The experiments do not tell you where the line is for your work; nobody can, because it moves with every model release. They tell you that the line exists and that the cost of not knowing where it is falls on the hardest task of the week, not the easiest.

What they do not say is as important: this is one session of work per participant, not a year of a reorganized office, and the P&G problems were ones the company had already framed. The jump from "a person with AI equals a pair" to "halve the team" is yours, not the paper's.

quote.text: individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI, demonstrating that AI can effectively replicate certain benefits of human collaboration
quote.where: Dell'Acqua et al., The Cybernetic Teammate, NBER Working Paper 33641 (2025), abstract

question.q: In the Procter and Gamble experiment, one person working with AI performed about as well as:
options: Two people working together without AI
Two people working together with AI
Nobody: AI users did worse on every measure
question.explain: The NBER abstract states that individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without AI. Teams with AI did better still, and AI users across the board produced more balanced solutions and reported more positive emotions.

days.do: Next time you draft something with a colleague from the other side of the house (economist and sector specialist, say), each of you run the problem through AI first and compare what it added. The silo finding is cheap to test.

figure.caption: Quality of the solution, in standard deviations above one person working alone without AI. A person with AI is a pair; a pair with AI is a slightly better pair.
figure.where: Dell'Acqua et al., The Cybernetic Teammate, NBER Working Paper 33641 (2025), Table 2, PDF page 14
figure.unit: Standard deviations over individuals without AI
figure.note: SD means standard deviations, the unit researchers use to compare different tests.

days.title: In the classroom: crutch or tutor
days.hook: Two randomized trials from the EvidencIA base, one in Ankara and one in Benin City, show the same technology harming and helping learning. The difference was the design.
days.lesson:
EvidencIA is an open base of studies on AI and learning, built by a network that the World Bank's education team is part of; each study is checked against the paper and rated by evidence level (level 1 means a verified randomized trial that measured learning on a test taken without AI). Two level 1 trials, read together, are the best short answer to "does AI help people learn?"

In Ankara, Bastani and colleagues (PNAS, 2025) randomized about 50 high school classes, 839 students, across four 90-minute maths sessions. Students with open access to GPT-4 during practice scored 48 percent higher on the practice problems. Then they sat a closed-book exam on the same topics at the end of the session and scored 17 percent lower than the students who had used textbooks and notes. A second arm, a GPT-4 tutor with the teacher's solutions that gave hints instead of answers, erased the harm but produced no gain on the exam. The authors' word for the first arm is crutch. The test was in the same session, so this is about what sticks in an afternoon, not a year.

In Benin City, De Simone and colleagues (World Bank, 2025) randomized 1,328 volunteer students in nine public schools. For six weeks, in pairs, after school, they used Microsoft Copilot as an English tutor with prompts the teachers had written so it would guide rather than answer, and trained teachers circulating in the room. English scores rose by 0.238 standard deviations on a curriculum test at the end, at about 48 dollars per student. The caveats are real: the treatment bundles extra time, supervision and AI, and 43 percent of students did not sit the final test, with more loss among controls. The authors are Bank colleagues, so the base says so next to the result.

Same technology, opposite outcomes. The variable was never the model. It was whether the design made the student do the thinking.

quote.text: Without guardrails, students attempt to use GPT-4 as a “crutch” during practice problem sessions, and subsequently perform worse on their own.
quote.where: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 122(26), 2025, abstract

question.q: In the Ankara trial, students with open access to GPT-4 during practice did what on the closed-book exam at the end of the session?
options: Scored about the same as the textbook group
question.explain: The 48 percent is the gain on the practice problems while the AI was open. On the unassisted exam the same students scored 17 percent below the control group. The tutor arm with hints instead of answers removed the harm but did not add a gain. Both numbers are in the paper's abstract and in the EvidencIA record.

days.do: Open redevidencia.org/papers on your phone: fifty of these studies, one a day, same guess-first format as this course. Or ask your AI, with EvidencIA connected, one question about your own sector and see whether it answers with a study or with an opinion.

figure.caption: Ankara high-school students against the no-AI class: big gains while the AI was there, a loss on the closed-book exam once it was gone. The tutor version erased the loss.
figure.where: Bastani et al., Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning, PNAS 122(26), 2025, abstract
figure.unit: Difference from the control class, percent

days.title: Inside Anthropic: agents six to one
days.hook: On 16 October Anthropic opened its own payroll, calendar, Slack and hiring records. The jobs that shrank first were the junior ones.
days.lesson:
On 16 October 2026 the Anthropic Institute published How employment is changing at Anthropic (Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff and McCrory), built from the company's own records: headcount, hiring score cards, agent telemetry, calendars, Slack, and 17 interviews. A frontier AI lab is not a ministry, and the authors say many of its practices cannot be copied. It is still the most detailed look yet at an organization that runs on AI agents.

Three numbers carry it. The share of junior staff in technical departments fell from 21 to 14 percent since early 2025, and the junior share of technical hires from 27 to 9. In March 2026 the hours worked by AI agents passed the hours worked by people, and by August the agents an employee directs worked six times as many hours as the employee. Code commits per engineer run at five times the pace of six months earlier, and lawyers, accounts payable and salespeople all show more output. The same engineer, followed over time, adds much more code after adopting agents, with no rise in lines later removed or reverted. The authors note that adopting the tools was not random, so treat the size with care.

The surprise is where the bottleneck moved. Agent sessions spend around 80 percent of their time waiting for a human. Reading everything the agents produce would take over half the week even for non-technical staff, so by spring 2026 a fifth of sessions were meta-work (specs, reviews of other agents, dashboards), up from a tenth in the fall. Written standing instructions for agents went from a few hundred to 8,500 in a year. The median employee spends 20 percent more time in meetings than a year ago. Hiring managers now write more about autonomy and judgment and less about domain expertise.

What the company did about it is the part for a ministry: an early warning system for jobs at risk, and redeployment inside before hiring outside. The authors add the honest line themselves: none of this helps the people who were never hired.

quote.text: This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week.
quote.where: Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff and McCrory, How employment is changing at Anthropic, The Anthropic Institute, 16 October 2026, Key findings, third bullet

question.q: By August 2026, how did the hours worked by the AI agents an Anthropic employee directs compare with the employee's own hours?
question.explain: Figure 2 of the report: agent hours passed human hours for the first time in March 2026, and by August the agents an employee directs worked six times as many hours as the employee. Most of that agent time, around 80 percent, is spent waiting for the human to answer.

days.do: Count the tasks you handed to an AI this week, then the minutes you spent reading what came back. If the second number is the bigger one, you are the bottleneck the report describes: write one standing instruction, a saved prompt, for the task you repeat most.

figure.caption: Junior positions as a share of Anthropic's technical departments, in headcount and in new hires, since early 2025.
figure.where: Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff and McCrory, How employment is changing at Anthropic, 16 October 2026, Figure 1 and the paragraph above it
figure.unit: Percent of technical staff and of technical hires
figure.note: By August 2026 the AI agents employees direct worked six times as many hours as the employees.
